tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

17	Drive the elite performance of championship-level athletic programs by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships.
18	Key Achievements 2024/2025
19	Scaled Data Collection and Athlete Monitoring by 60% - Collected 1,000+ data sessions across eight platforms, enabling evidence-based training decisions and injury risk mitigation across the athletic department.

21	Implemented Advanced Performance Technologies Across Multiple Sports - Successfully deployed ForceFrame muscle force testing and Kinexon player tracking systems in Fall 2024, serving Football, Men's and Women's Basketball, and Olympic Sports programs, providing previously unavailable objective metrics that enhanced return-to-play protocols, workload management, and data-driven communication with coaching and medical staff.
22	Strategic Vision
23	We will serve as a project-based group, without specific sport assignments. Instead, the department will consist of content matter experts serving the following areas: biomechanics, exercise physiology, performance technology, and data science.
24	Our objective will be to solicit questions from key stakeholders to address specific needs and/or unique questions that arise throughout the season/year.

26	Student-athlete and staff education.

31	
32	1.1 Performance Metrics & Analytics
33	Quantitative Impact
34	1.2 Success Stories & Case Studies
35	Case Study 1: Facility Transition
36	Sport: Football
37	Challenge: Team transitioned from afternoon to morning practices in a new facility, raising concerns about potential decreases in practice intensity and quality with the schedule change.
38	Intervention: Conducted GPS analysis comparing key performance metrics before and after the transition. Implemented weekly Thursday practice top-ups to ensure athletes achieved ≥90% maximum velocity efforts before competition.
39	Outcome: Data revealed no drop-off in practice intensity during morning sessions. Athletes demonstrated equal or improved speed metrics in the new timeframe. Thursday top-ups ensured that 100% of athletes met the 90% max velocity threshold each week, validating the schedule change and establishing a sustainable training model.
40	Case Study 2: Load Monitoring Implementation
41	Sport: Volleyball
42	Challenge: Lack of objective data to identify periods where competition schedule demands and weekly training load were misaligned, potentially increasing injury risk and compromising athlete readiness.
43	Intervention: Implemented session RPE (sRPE) tracking throughout the season, converting responses into training load scores. Monitored data weekly to identify high-load periods and schedule training misalignments and used findings to advocate for practice modifications during congested competitive windows.
44	Outcome: Successfully identified multiple periods of load-schedule misalignment during the season. Data-driven insights enabled the strength coach to secure practice modifications, better managing the athlete workload. Post-season analysis quantified sRPE-training load relationships, providing coaching staff with evidence-based frameworks for future season planning and load management strategies.
45	1.3 Technology & Innovation Implementations
46	New Technologies Deployed
47	Force Frame
48	Implementation Date: Fall 2024
49	Sports Utilizing: Football, Basketball (M/W), Olympic Sports
50	Impact: ForceFrame muscle force testing has enhanced our athlete monitoring and return-to-play protocols by streamlining assessment efficiency and providing previously unavailable objective force metrics. Technology has improved decision-making on training modifications, return-to-play timelines, and load management, providing coaching and medical staff with quantifiable data to guide athlete readiness and recovery across multiple sports.
51	
52	Kinexon
53	Implementation Date: Fall 2024
54	Sports Utilizing: Women's Basketball
55	Impact: Kinexon player tracking has transformed our approach to athlete monitoring by quantifying practice volume, intensity, and density across training sessions. The system provides objective metrics for athlete profiling and return-to-play protocols, enabling data-driven decisions around workload management and readiness. These insights have enhanced communication with coaching staff, supporting evidence-based adjustments to practice design and individualized load management strategies.
56	Data Integration Achievements
57	Our department has integrated multiple data streams, including player-tracking metrics, force assessments, subjective load monitoring, and performance testing, to create a comprehensive athlete-monitoring system. This integrated approach enables cross-referencing of external training loads with internal responses and neuromuscular status, providing a holistic view of athlete readiness.
58	
59	SECTION 2: DEPARTMENT OPERATIONS
60	
61	2.1 Organizational Structure
62	Director of Applied Sport Science: Eric Rash
63	Credentials: MS, SCCC, CPSS (Pursuing)
64	Areas of Expertise: Strategic vision, vendor relations, Innovation, and Research initiatives

67	Credentials: MS, CSCS, CPSS (Pursuing)
68	Areas of Expertise: Logistical support and system operations

70	Undergraduate Interns: 1 (Andrew McKowen)

72	Core Services
73	Performance Testing & Assessment
74	Performance testing is integrated into scheduled lifting sessions to monitor physical development and readiness. Force plate assessments are conducted weekly for most teams to track neuromuscular function and jump performance. 
75	Mid-thigh pull testing is performed weekly to monthly, depending on the sport and season phase, to evaluate maximal force production. This testing frequency balances longitudinal data collection with minimal disruption to training, enabling trend analysis and informed programming decisions throughout the year.
76	Training Load Monitoring
77	Comprehensive multi-device monitoring ecosystem to track athlete training load and readiness across 14 sports. The department collected 1000+ data sessions across eight platforms. This centralized data-collection approach enables evidence-based training decisions, load management, and injury-risk mitigation across the athletic department.
78	Data Analytics & Reporting
79	Regular performance reports and dashboards utilizing data from multiple platforms to inform coaching decisions and track athlete development.
80	Analytics deliverables support daily training decisions, weekly load management, and longitudinal performance tracking.
81	Research & Innovation
82	Actively engaged with HHPR on several different initiatives. Most center on traditional research projects that lead to publication.
83	Beyond the active research taking place, Athletics staff serve as adjunct faculty in the spring semester, instructing the course HP5355

87	Robbins College: HHPR

94	Baseball – Sleep Metrics: Athletes averaged 7.3 hours of sleep with 89% sleep efficiency during fall training.
